Jeremiah 42:9; Daniel 9:18; Jeremiah 42:2; 2 Kings 19:4; Psalm 144:2.

Here several questions are raised by way of objection. Scripture relates that God sometimes granted certain prayers which had been prompted by minds that were not properly calmed or governed. It is true that the cause for which Jotham called down on the inhabitants of Shechem the disaster which later befell them was well founded; but he was still inflamed with anger and revenge (Judges 9:20); and so God, by granting the curse, seems to approve of passionate impulses. A similar heat also seized Samson when he prayed, "Strengthen me, I pray you, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes" (Judges 16:28). For although there was some mixture of good zeal, his ruling feeling was a fiery, and therefore sinful, longing for vengeance. God grants it, and so it might apparently be inferred that prayers are effective even when they are not framed according to the rule of the word. But I answer, first, that a perpetual law is not abolished by isolated examples; and, secondly, that special promptings have sometimes been given to a few individuals, whose case is thereby different from that of men in general. For we should note the answer which our Savior gave to his disciples when they thoughtlessly wished to imitate the example of Elijah: "You know not what manner of spirit you are of" (Luke 9:55). We must, however, go further and say that the wishes which God grants are not always pleasing to him; but he grants them because it is necessary, by way of example, to give clear proof of the doctrine of Scripture, namely, that he helps the wretched and hears the groans of those who, being unjustly afflicted, beg for his aid; and accordingly he carries out his judgments when the complaints of the needy rise to him, though in themselves they are unworthy of attention. For how often, in punishing the ungodly for cruelty, plunder, violence, lust, and other crimes, in curbing audacity and fury, and also in overthrowing tyrannical power, has he declared that he gives help to those who are undeservedly oppressed, even though by calling on an unknown deity they only beat the air? There is one psalm which clearly teaches that prayers are not without effect even though they do not reach heaven by faith (Psalm 107:6, 13, 19). For it lists the prayers which, by natural instinct, need wrings from unbelievers no less than from believers, and it shows by the outcome that God is nevertheless favorable to them. Is it to testify by such readiness to hear that their prayers are pleasing to him? Not at all; it is, first, to magnify and display his mercy by the fact that even the wishes of unbelievers are not refused; and, secondly, to stir up his true worshipers to more urgent prayer, when they see that sometimes even the wailings of the ungodly are not without effect. This, however, is no reason why believers should depart from the law divinely laid upon them, or envy unbelievers, as if they gained much in obtaining what they wished. We have observed (chapter 3, section 25) that in this way God yielded to the feigned repentance of Ahab, in order to show how ready he is to listen to his elect when they seek his favor with true contrition. Accordingly, he rebukes the Jews because, soon after experiencing his readiness to listen to their prayers, they returned to their own perverse inclinations. It is also plain from the Book of Judges that whenever they wept, though their tears were deceitful, they were delivered from the hands of their enemies. Therefore, as God sends his sun without distinction on the evil and on the good, so he does not despise the tears of those who have a good cause and whose sorrows deserve relief. Meanwhile, though he hears them, this has no more to do with salvation than the supply of food which he gives to other despisers of his goodness. There seems to be a more difficult question concerning Abraham and Samuel, the first of whom, without any instruction from the word of God, prayed on behalf of the people of Sodom, while the other, against an express prohibition, prayed on behalf of Saul (Genesis 18:23; 1 Samuel 15:11). The case of Jeremiah is similar, who prayed that the city might not be destroyed (Jeremiah 32:16). It is true that their prayers were refused, but it seems harsh to assert that they prayed without faith. Modest readers will, I hope, be satisfied with this solution, namely, that, relying on the general principle by which God commands us to be merciful even to the unworthy, they were not wholly without faith, though in this particular case their wish was disappointed. Augustine shrewdly remarks, "How do the saints pray in faith when they ask of God what is contrary to what he has decreed? Namely, because they pray according to his will, not his hidden and unchangeable will, but that which he suggests to them, so that he may hear them in another way; as he wisely distinguishes" (Augustine, City of God, book 22, chapter 2). This is truly said: for in his incomprehensible counsel he so governs events that the prayers of the saints, though they involve a mixture of faith and error, are not in vain. And yet this no more warrants imitation than it excuses the saints themselves, who, I do not deny, went beyond proper bounds. Therefore, whenever no certain promise exists, our request to God must have a condition attached to it. Here we may refer to the prayer of David, "Awake for me to the judgment that you have commanded" (Psalm 7:6); for he reminds us that he had received special instruction to pray for a temporal blessing. The French adds, "dequel il n'eust pas autrement esté asseuré;" that is, of which he would not otherwise have felt assured.

It is also important to note that the four laws of prayer which I have discussed are not so rigorously enforced that God rejects the prayers in which he does not find perfect faith or repentance, accompanied by fervent zeal and rightly ordered desires. We have said (section 4) that though prayer is the familiar communion of believers with God, reverence and modesty must still be observed: we must not give free rein to our wishes, nor long for anything beyond what God permits; and, moreover, so that the majesty of God may not be despised, our minds must be lifted up to a pure and chaste reverence. No man has ever done this with complete perfection. For, not to speak of men in general, how often do David's complaints smack of excess? Not that he actually means to argue with God or to grumble at his judgments, but, faltering through weakness, he finds no better comfort than to pour his griefs into the bosom of his heavenly Father. Indeed, God bears even with our stammering, and pardon is granted to our ignorance as often as anything rash escapes us; in fact, without this indulgence we should have no freedom to pray. But although it was David's intention to submit himself entirely to the will of God, and he prayed with no less patience than fervor, still disordered emotions appear, indeed sometimes burst out, emotions not a little at odds with the first law we laid down. In particular, we may see in a verse of the thirty-ninth Psalm how this saint was carried away by the force of his grief and was unable to keep within bounds. "O spare me." Latin, "Desine a me." French, "Retire-toy"; that is, Withdraw from me.

But since no man is worthy to come forward in his own name and appear in the presence of God, our heavenly Father, to free us at once from the fear and shame with which all must feel weighed down... French, "Confusion que nous avons, ou devons avoir en nousmesmes"; that is, the confusion which we have, or ought to have, in ourselves.

And we must pay careful attention to the matter of time. Christ commands his disciples to have recourse to his intercession after he has ascended to heaven: "At that day you shall ask in my name" (John 16:26). It is certain, indeed, that from the very beginning all who ever prayed were heard only for the sake of the Mediator. For this reason God had commanded in the Law that the priest alone should enter the sanctuary, bearing the names of the twelve tribes of Israel on his shoulders and as many precious stones on his breast, while the people were to stand at a distance in the outer court and then join their prayers with the priest's. Indeed, the sacrifice even served to ratify and confirm their prayers. That shadowy ceremony of the Law therefore taught, first, that we are all shut out from the face of God, and that there is therefore need of a Mediator to appear in our name, to carry us on his shoulders and keep us bound upon his breast, so that we may be heard in his person; and, secondly, that our prayers, which, as has been said, would otherwise never be free from impurity, are cleansed by the sprinkling of his blood. And we see that the saints, when they desired to obtain anything, based their hopes on sacrifices, because they knew that all prayers were ratified by sacrifice: "Remember all your offerings," says David, "and accept your burnt sacrifice" (Psalm 20:3). From this we infer that, in receiving the prayers of his people, God was from the very beginning appeased by the intercession of Christ. Why then does Christ speak of a new period ("at that day") when the disciples were to begin to pray in his name, unless it is that this grace, being now more brightly displayed, ought also to be held in higher esteem by us? In this sense he had said a little before, "Hitherto have you asked nothing in my name: ask." Not that they were wholly ignorant of the office of Mediator (all the Jews were instructed in these first rudiments), but they did not clearly understand that Christ, by his ascension to heaven, would be the advocate of the Church more than before. Therefore, to relieve their grief at his absence by some more than ordinary benefit, he asserts his office of advocate and says that until then they had been without the special benefit which it would be their privilege to enjoy when, aided by his intercession, they would call upon God with greater freedom. In this sense the Apostle says that we have "boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he has consecrated for us" (Hebrews 10:19, 20). All the more inexcusable, therefore, are we if we do not embrace with both hands (as the saying goes) the priceless gift which is properly intended for us.

Moreover, since he himself is the only way and the only access by which we can draw near to God, those who stray from this way and refuse this access have no other left; his throne offers them nothing but wrath, judgment, and terror. In short, since the Father has consecrated him as our guide and head, those who abandon him or turn aside from him in any way are trying, as far as lies in them, to stain and erase the seal which God has stamped. Christ, therefore, is the only Mediator by whose intercession the Father is made favorable and willing to be entreated (1 Timothy 2:5). For though the saints are still permitted to use intercessions, by which they plead with God for one another's salvation, and which the Apostle mentions (Ephesians 6:18, 19; 1 Timothy 2:1), yet these depend on that one intercession, so far are they from detracting from it. For just as the intercessions which we offer up for one another, as members of one body, spring from the feeling of love, so they look to this one head. Since they are thus also made in the name of Christ, what more do they do than declare that no one can gain the least benefit from any prayers without the intercession of Christ? As there is nothing in the intercession of Christ to prevent the different members of the Church from offering up prayers for one another, so let it be held as a fixed principle that all the intercessions used in this way in the Church must look to that one intercession. Indeed, we must be especially careful to show our gratitude on this very account, that God, pardoning our unworthiness, not only allows each individual to pray for himself but allows all to intercede for one another. Since God has given a place in his Church to intercessors who would deserve to be rejected if they prayed privately on their own account, how presumptuous would it be to abuse this kindness by using it to obscure the honor of Christ?

Moreover, the Sophists are guilty of the merest trifling when they claim that Christ is the Mediator of redemption, but that believers are mediators of intercession; as if Christ had performed only a temporary mediation and left an eternal and imperishable mediation to his servants. Such, to be sure, is the treatment he receives from those who pretend to take from him only a tiny portion of honor. Very different is the language of Scripture, with whose simplicity every godly man will be satisfied, paying no regard to those impostors. For when John says, "If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1), does he mean merely that we once had an advocate? Does he not rather ascribe to him a perpetual intercession? What does Paul mean when he declares that he "is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us" (Romans 8:32)? And when in another passage he declares that he is the only Mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5), is he not referring to the supplications he had mentioned a little before? Having first said that prayers were to be offered for all men, he immediately adds, in confirmation of that statement, that there is one God and one Mediator between God and man. Nor does Augustine give a different interpretation when he says: "Christian men commend one another in their prayers. But he for whom no one intercedes, while he himself intercedes for all, is the only true Mediator. Though the Apostle Paul was a principal member under the head, yet because he was a member of the body of Christ, and knew that the most true and High Priest of the Church had entered, not in figure into the inner veil of the holy of holies, but in firm and express truth into the inner sanctuary of heaven, to a holiness not imaginary but eternal, he too commends himself to the prayers of the faithful. He does not make himself a mediator between God and the people, but asks that all the members of the body of Christ should pray for one another, since the members share one another's feelings: if one member suffers, the others suffer with it. And so the mutual prayers of all the members still laboring on earth ascend to the Head, who has gone before into heaven, and in whom there is propitiation for our sins. For if Paul were a mediator, so would the other apostles be, and so there would be many mediators, and Paul's statement could not stand, 'There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus'; in whom we also are one if we keep the unity of the faith in the bond of peace." Hebrews 9:11, 24; Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19; Colossians 4:3; 1 Corinthians 12:25; 1 Timothy 2:5; Ephesians 4:3.

As for the saints who, having died in the body, live in Christ, if we attribute prayer to them, let us not imagine that they have any other way of making supplication to God than through Christ, who alone is the way, or that their prayers are accepted by God in any other name. Therefore, since Scripture calls us away from all others to Christ alone, and since our heavenly Father is pleased to gather together all things in him, it would be the height of stupidity, not to say madness, to try to gain access through others, so as to be drawn away from him without whom access cannot be gained. But who can deny that this was the practice for several ages, and is still the practice wherever Popery prevails? To win the favor of God, human merits are thrust forward again and again, and very often, while Christ is passed by, God is petitioned in their name. I ask whether this is not to transfer to them that office of sole intercession which we have claimed above for Christ? Then what angel or devil ever announced one syllable to any human being about that imagined intercession of theirs? There is not a word on the subject in Scripture. What ground, then, was there for the invention? Certainly, when the human mind seeks for itself help that is not sanctioned by the word of God, it plainly displays its distrust (see section 27). But if we appeal to the consciences of all who take pleasure in the intercession of saints, we shall find that their only reason for it is that they are filled with anxiety, as if they supposed that Christ were insufficient or too severe. By this anxiety they dishonor Christ and rob him of his title of sole Mediator, a title which, having been given him by the Father as his special privilege, ought not to be transferred to any other. By doing so they obscure the glory of his birth and make his cross void; in short, they strip and defraud of its due praise everything he did or suffered, since all that he did and suffered goes to show that he is, and ought to be regarded as, the sole Mediator. At the same time, they reject the kindness of God in revealing himself to them as a Father, for he is not their Father if they do not acknowledge Christ as their brother. This they plainly refuse to do if they do not believe that he feels for them a brother's affection, an affection more gentle and tender than any other. Therefore Scripture offers him alone, sends us to him, and establishes us in him. "He," says Ambrose, "is our mouth, by which we speak to the Father; our eye, by which we see the Father; our right hand, by which we offer ourselves to the Father. Apart from his intercession neither we nor any saints have any communion with God" (Ambrose, On Isaac and the Soul). If they object that the public prayers offered in churches end with the words, through Jesus Christ our Lord, it is a frivolous evasion; for no less insult is done to the intercession of Christ by mixing it up with the prayers and merits of the dead than by leaving it out altogether and mentioning only the dead. Besides, in all their litanies, hymns, and proses, where every kind of honor is paid to dead saints, there is no mention of Christ.

But here stupidity has gone so far as to display the true character of superstition, which, once it has thrown off the reins, is accustomed to run riot without limit. After men began to look to the intercession of saints, a particular department was gradually assigned to each, so that, according to the variety of business, now one intercessor and now another was called upon. Then individuals adopted particular saints and put their faith in them, just as if they had been guardian deities. And so gods were set up not only according to the number of the cities (the charge which the prophet brought against Israel of old, Jeremiah 2:28; 11:13), but according to the number of individuals. But while the saints, in all their desires, refer to the will of God alone, look to it, and rest in it, to assign them any other prayer than that of longing for the coming of the kingdom of God is to think of them foolishly, carnally, and even insultingly. Nothing could be further from such a view than to imagine that each of them, moved by private feeling, is inclined to be most favorable to his own worshipers. At length vast numbers have fallen into the horrid blasphemy of calling on them not merely as helpers but as presiding over their salvation. See the depth to which miserable men fall when they forsake their proper station, that is, the word of God. I say nothing of the more monstrous examples of impiety in which, though they are detestable to God, angels, and men, they themselves feel no pain or shame. Bowing down before a statue or picture of Barbara or Catherine and the like, they mutter a Pater Noster. Erasmus, though stumbling and walking blindfolded in clear light, ventures to write thus in a letter to Sadolet, 1530: "Primum, constat nullum esse locum in divinis voluminibus, qui permittat invocare divcs, nisi fortasse detorquere huc placte, quod dives in Evangelica parabola implorat opem Abrahæ. Quanquam autem in re tanta novare quicquam præter auctoritatem Scripturæ, merito, periculosum videri possit, tamen invocationem divorum nusquam improbo," etc. That is: First, it is clear that there is no passage in the sacred volume which permits the invocation of saints, unless we choose to twist to this purpose what is said in the parable about the rich man begging the help of Abraham. But though in so weighty a matter it may rightly seem dangerous to introduce anything without the authority of Scripture, I by no means condemn the invocation of saints, etc.
Latin, "Pastores"; French, "ceux qui se disent prelats, curés ou precheurs"; that is, those who call themselves prelates, curates, or preachers.

French, "Mais encore qu'ils taschent de laver leur mains d'un si vilain sacrilege, conleur qu'il ne se commet point en leurs serviteurs pour les aider? mesmes o˜ ils supplient la vierge Maire de commander a son fils qu'il leur ottroye leur requestes?" That is: But although they try to wash their hands of so vile a sacrilege, since it is not committed in their masses or vespers, under what pretext will they defend those blasphemies which they repeat at the top of their voices, in which they pray St. Eloy or St. Medard to look down from heaven upon their servants and help them, and even beg the Virgin Mary to command her Son to grant their requests?

They labor in vain in trying to prove that such intercession has some support in Scripture. We often read, they say, of the prayers of angels; and not only so, but the prayers of believers are said to be carried into the presence of God by their hands. But if they would compare saints who have departed this life with angels, they will have to prove that the saints are ministering spirits, to whom has been entrusted the office of watching over our salvation, to whom has been assigned the task of guiding us in all our ways, of surrounding, admonishing, and comforting us, and of keeping watch over us. All these duties are assigned to angels, but none of them to saints. How absurdly they confuse departed saints with angels is evident enough from the many different offices by which Scripture distinguishes the one from the other. No one will presume to act as an advocate before an earthly judge unless he has been admitted to do so; where, then, do worms get such license as to thrust themselves upon God as intercessors, when no such office has been assigned them? God has been pleased to give angels the charge of our safety. Therefore they attend our sacred assemblies, and the Church is to them a theater in which they behold the manifold wisdom of God (Ephesians 3:10). Those who transfer to others this office which belongs peculiarly to the angels certainly pervert and confuse the order which God has established and which ought to be inviolable. With similar skill they go on to quote other passages. God said to Jeremiah, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people" (Jeremiah 15:1). How, they ask, could he have spoken this way of the dead, unless he knew that they interceded for the living? My inference, on the contrary, is this: since it appears from this that neither Moses nor Samuel interceded for the people of Israel, there was then no intercession by the dead. For which of the saints can be supposed to labor for the salvation of the people while Moses, who in his lifetime far surpassed all others in this matter, does nothing? Therefore, if they persist in the petty quibble that the dead intercede for the living because the Lord said, "If they stood before me" (intercesserint), I will argue far more plausibly in this way: Moses, of whom it is said, "if he interceded," did not intercede for the people in their extreme need; it is probable, therefore, that no other saint intercedes, since all fall far behind Moses in humanity, goodness, and fatherly care. So all they gain by their quibbling is to be wounded by the very weapons with which they think themselves so admirably protected. But it is quite ridiculous to twist this simple sentence in this way; for the Lord only declares that he would not spare the iniquities of the people even if some Moses or Samuel, to whose prayers he had shown himself so indulgent, were to intercede for them. This meaning comes out most clearly from a similar passage in Ezekiel: "Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord God" (Ezekiel 14:14). Here there can be no doubt that we are to understand the words as if it had been said, If two of the persons named were to come back to life; for the third, namely Daniel, was still living, who, as is well known, had then, in the bloom of youth, given an incomparable display of godliness. Let us therefore leave out those whom Scripture declares to have finished their course. Accordingly, when Paul speaks of David, he does not say that he helped posterity by his prayers, but only that he "served his own generation" (Acts 13:36).

They object again: Are those, then, to be deprived of every godly wish who, during the whole course of their lives, breathed nothing but godliness and mercy? I have no wish to pry curiously into what they do or think; but the probability is that, instead of being moved by various and particular desires, they long with one fixed and unchanging will for the kingdom of God, which consists no less in the destruction of the ungodly than in the salvation of believers. If this is so, there can be no doubt that their love is confined to the communion of Christ's body and extends no further than is compatible with the nature of that communion. But though I grant that in this way they pray for us, they do not, however, lose their rest so as to be distracted by earthly cares; much less, then, are they to be called upon by us. Nor does it follow that such invocation is to be practiced because men, while they are alive on earth, can commend themselves to one another's prayers. That practice serves to keep alive a feeling of love, as they, so to speak, share one another's needs and bear one another's burdens. They do this by the command of the Lord, and not without a promise, the two things of first importance in prayer. But all such reasons do not apply to the dead, with whom the Lord, in withdrawing them from our company, has left us no means of communication (Ecclesiastes 9:5, 6), and to whom, as far as we can guess, he has left no means of communication with us. But if anyone claims that they must surely keep the same love for us, since they are united with us in one faith, who has revealed to us that they have ears able to hear the sound of our voice, or eyes clear enough to see our needs? Our opponents, indeed, talk in the shade of their schools of some kind of light which shines on departed saints from the face of God, and in which, as in a mirror, they behold the affairs of men from their lofty dwelling; but to assert this with the confidence these men presume to use is simply to desire, by means of the extravagant dreams of our own brain and without any authority, to pry and break into the hidden judgments of God, and to trample on Scripture, which so often declares that the wisdom of our flesh is at enmity with the wisdom of God, utterly condemns the vanity of our mind, and, humbling our reason, bids us look only to the will of God.

The other passages of Scripture which they use to defend their error are miserably twisted. Jacob, they say, asks for the sons of Joseph, "Let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac" (Genesis 48:16). First, let us see what the nature of this invocation was among the Israelites. They do not beg their fathers to bring them help, but they plead with God to remember his servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Their example, therefore, gives no support to those who direct their addresses to the saints themselves. But since these blockheads are so dull that they do not understand what it is to invoke the name of Jacob, or why it is to be invoked, it is no wonder that they blunder so childishly about the way of doing it. The expression occurs repeatedly in Scripture. Isaiah speaks of women being called by the name of men when they have them as husbands and live under their protection (Isaiah 4:1). The calling of the name of Abraham over the Israelites consists in tracing the origin of their race to him and holding him in honored remembrance as their founder and parent. Jacob does not do this out of any eagerness to spread the fame of his name, but because he knows that all the happiness of his descendants lay in their inheriting the covenant which God had made with them. Seeing that this would give them the sum of all blessings, he prays that they may be counted as of his race, which is nothing else than to hand on the succession of the covenant to them. They in turn, when they mention this in their prayers, do not resort to the intercession of the dead, but call to mind that covenant in which their most merciful Father undertakes to be kind and favorable to them for the sake of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. How little, in other respects, the saints trusted in the merits of their fathers is declared by the public voice of the Church in the prophets: "Doubtless you are our Father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: you, O Lord, are our Father, our Redeemer" (Isaiah 63:16). And while the Church speaks this way, she at the same time adds, "Return for your servants' sake," not thinking of anything like intercession, but looking only to the benefit of the covenant. Now indeed, when we have the Lord Jesus, in whose hand the eternal covenant of mercy was not only made but confirmed, what better name can we carry before us in our prayers? And since those good Doctors would make out from these words that the Patriarchs are intercessors, I should like them to tell me why, in so great a multitude... The French adds, "et quasi en une fourmiliere de saincts"; that is, and as it were a swarm of saints.
"C'est chose trop notoire de quel bourbieu de quelle racaille ils tirent leur saincts." That is: It is all too well known out of what mire or rubbish they draw their saints.

But some seem to be moved by the fact that the prayers of saints are often said to have been heard. Why were they heard? Because they prayed. "They cried unto you," says the Psalmist, "and were delivered: they trusted in you, and were not confounded" (Psalm 22:5). Let us also pray after their example, so that like them we too may be heard. These men, on the contrary, absurdly argue that none will be heard but those who have been heard already. How much better James argues: "Elijah was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit" (James 5:17, 18). What? Does he infer that Elijah possessed some special privilege, and that we must resort to him to make use of it? By no means. He shows the perpetual power of a pure and godly prayer, so that we may be moved to pray in the same way. For the kindness and readiness of God to hear others is maliciously misinterpreted if their example does not inspire us with stronger confidence in his promise, since his declaration is not that he will incline his ear to one or two or a few individuals, but to all who call upon his name. They are all the less excusable in this ignorance, because they seem, as it were, openly to despise the many warnings of Scripture. David was repeatedly delivered by the power of God. Was this to hand that power over to him, so that we might be delivered at his request? Very different is his own statement: "The righteous shall compass me about; for you shall deal bountifully with me" (Psalm 142:7). Again, "The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him" (Psalm 52:6). "This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles" (Psalm 34:6). In the Psalms there are many similar prayers in which David calls on God to give him what he asks for this reason, namely, that the righteous may not be put to shame, but may be encouraged by his example to hope. Here let one passage suffice: "For this shall every one that is godly pray unto you in a time when you may be found" (Psalm 32:6, Calvin's Commentary). I have quoted this passage the more readily because those ravers who hire out their tongues in defense of the Papacy are not ashamed to bring it forward as proof of the intercession of the dead. As if David meant anything more than to show the benefit he will gain from the divine mercy and condescension when he has been heard! In general, we must hold that the experience of the grace of God, toward ourselves as well as toward others, does much to strengthen our faith in his promises. I do not quote the many passages in which David sets forth God's loving-kindness to him as a ground of confidence, since they will readily occur to every reader of the Psalms. Jacob had earlier taught the same thing by his own example: "I am not worthy of the least of all your mercies, and of all the truth which you have showed unto your servant; for with my staff I passed over this Jordan; and now I am become two bands" (Genesis 32:10). He does indeed plead the promise, but not the promise only; for he adds at the same time its effect, to fill himself with greater confidence in the future kindness of God. God is not like men, who grow weary of their generosity or whose means of exercising it run out; but he is to be judged by his own nature, as David rightly does when he says, "You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth" (Psalm 31:5). After giving God the praise for his salvation, he adds that he is true; for if he were not always like himself, his past favor would not be a sure ground for confidence and prayer. But when we know that as often as he helps us he gives us a sample and proof of his goodness and faithfulness, there is no reason to fear that our hope will be put to shame or frustrated.

On the whole, since Scripture places the chief part of worship in calling upon God (this being the duty of godliness which he requires of us in preference to all sacrifices), it is plain sacrilege to offer prayer to others. Hence it is said in the psalm: "If we have forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a strange god; shall not God search this out?" (Psalm 44:20, 21). Again, since God desires to be called upon only in faith, and he expressly commands us to frame our prayers according to the rule of his word; in short, since faith is founded on the word and is the parent of right prayer, the moment we turn aside from the word our prayers are impure. But we have already shown that if we consult the whole volume of Scripture, we shall find that God claims this honor for himself alone. As to the office of intercession, we have also seen that it belongs peculiarly to Christ, and that no prayer is pleasing to God which he, as Mediator, does not sanctify. And though believers offer up prayers to God on behalf of their brethren, we have shown that this in no way detracts from the sole intercession of Christ, because all rely on that intercession in commending themselves as well as others to God. Moreover, we have shown that this is ignorantly transferred to the dead, of whom we nowhere read that they were commanded to pray for us. Scripture often urges us to pray for one another, but says not one syllable about the dead; indeed, James implicitly excludes the dead when he joins the two things, to "confess our sins one to another, and to pray one for another" (James 5:16). It is enough, then, to condemn this error that the beginning of right prayer springs from faith, and that faith comes by hearing the word of God, in which there is no mention of invented intercession, superstition having rashly adopted intercessors who have not been divinely appointed. While Scripture abounds in various forms of prayer, we find no example of this intercession, without which the Papists think there is no prayer. Moreover, it is evident that this superstition is the fruit of distrust, because they are either not content with Christ as intercessor or have robbed him of this honor altogether. The latter is easily proved by their brazenness in maintaining, as the strongest of all their arguments for the intercession of the saints, that we are unworthy of familiar access to God. This, indeed, we acknowledge to be entirely true, but we infer from it that they leave nothing to Christ, because they count his intercession as nothing unless it is supplemented by that of George and Hippolytus and similar phantoms.

But though prayer is properly confined to vows and supplications, yet so close is the kinship between petition and thanksgiving that both may conveniently be included under one name. For the forms which Paul lists (1 Timothy 2:1) fall under the first member of this division. By prayer and supplication we pour out our desires before God, asking both for those things which serve to promote his glory and display his name, and for the benefits which contribute to our own good. By thanksgiving we rightly celebrate his kindnesses toward us, ascribing to his generosity every blessing that falls to our lot. David accordingly includes both in one sentence: "Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me" (Psalm 50:15). Not without reason, Scripture commands us to use both continually. We have already described how great our need is, while experience itself proclaims that the straits pressing on us from every side are so many and so great that all have ample reason to send up sighs and groans to God without ceasing and to beg him humbly. For even if they should be free from adversity, the holiest ought still to be driven, first by their sins and secondly by the countless assaults of temptation, to long for a remedy. The sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving can never be interrupted without guilt, since God never ceases to heap favor upon favor on us, so as to compel us to gratitude, however slow and sluggish we may be. In short, so great and so widely spread are the riches of his generosity toward us, so marvelous and wonderful the miracles we behold on every side, that we can never lack a subject and material for praise and thanksgiving. To make this somewhat clearer: since all our hopes and resources are placed in God (this has already been fully proved), so that neither our persons nor our interests can prosper without his blessing, we must constantly submit ourselves and all we have to him. Then whatever we consider, say, or do should be considered, said, and done under his hand and will; in short, in the hope of his help. God has pronounced a curse on all who, trusting in themselves or in others, form plans and resolutions, who, without regard to his will and without calling on his help, either plan or attempt to carry out anything (James 4:14; Isaiah 30:1; 31:1). And since, as has already been observed, he receives the honor due to him when he is acknowledged to be the author of all good, it follows that, as we receive all good from his hand, we ought continually to express our thankfulness, and that we have no right to use the benefits which come from his generosity unless we diligently proclaim his praise and give him thanks, these being the ends for which they are given. When Paul declares that every creature of God "is sanctified by the word of God and prayers" (1 Timothy 4:5), he indicates that without the word and prayers none of them is holy and pure, word being used by metonymy for faith. Therefore David, on experiencing the loving-kindness of the Lord, beautifully declares, "He has put a new song in my mouth" (Psalm 40:3), indicating that our silence is malicious when we leave his blessings unpraised, since every blessing he bestows is a new ground for thanksgiving. So Isaiah, proclaiming the singular mercies of God, says, "Sing unto the Lord a new song" (Isaiah 42:10). In the same sense David says in another passage, "O Lord, open my lips; and my mouth shall show forth your praise" (Psalm 51:15). Likewise Hezekiah and Jonah declare that they will regard it as the purpose of their deliverance "to celebrate the goodness of God with songs in his temple" (Isaiah 38:20; Jonah 2:10). David lays down a general rule for all believers in these words: "What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord" (Psalm 116:12, 13). The Church follows this rule in another psalm: "Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto your holy name, and to triumph in your praise" (Psalm 106:47). Again, "He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer. This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the Lord." "To declare the name of the Lord in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem" (Psalm 102:18, 21). Indeed, whenever believers beseech the Lord to do anything for his own name's sake, just as they declare themselves unworthy of obtaining it in their own name, so they bind themselves to give thanks and promise to make right use of his loving-kindness by being its heralds. So Hosea, speaking of the future redemption of the Church, says, "Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips" (Hosea 14:2). Not only do our tongues proclaim the kindness of God, but that kindness naturally inspires us with love for him: "I love the Lord, because he has heard my voice and my supplications" (Psalm 116:1). In another passage, speaking of the help he had experienced, he says, "I will love you, O Lord, my strength" (Psalm 18:1). No praise will ever please God that does not flow from this feeling of love. Indeed, we must heed the declaration of Paul that all desires are sinful and perverse which are not accompanied by thanksgiving. His words are, "In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Philippians 4:6). Because many, under the influence of sullenness, weariness, impatience, bitter grief, and fear, mingle grumbling with their prayers, he commands us so to govern our feelings that we cheerfully bless God even before we obtain what we ask. But if this connection ought always to remain in full force between things that are almost opposite, all the more sacred is the bond which obliges us to celebrate the praises of God whenever he grants our requests. And as we have already shown that our prayers, which would otherwise be polluted, are sanctified by the intercession of Christ, so the Apostle, by commanding us "to offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually" through Christ (Hebrews 13:15), reminds us that without the intervention of his priesthood our lips are not pure enough to celebrate the name of God. From this we infer that a monstrous delusion prevails among the Papists, the great majority of whom are astonished when Christ is called an intercessor. The reason Paul commands, "Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks" (1 Thessalonians 5:17, 18), is that he would have us, with the utmost diligence, at all times, in every place, in all things, and under all circumstances, direct our prayers to God, expect from him all the things we desire, and, when we have obtained them, ascribe them to him; thus providing perpetual grounds for prayer and praise.

This diligence in prayer, though it refers especially to the private prayers of individuals, also extends in some measure to the public prayers of the Church. These, it may be said, cannot be continual, and ought not to be offered except in the manner which, for the sake of order, has been established by common consent. This I grant, and that is why certain hours are fixed beforehand, hours which, though indifferent with respect to God, are necessary for the use of men, so that the general convenience may be served and all things may be done in the Church, as Paul commands, "decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40). But there is nothing in this to prevent each church from being stirred up now and then to a more frequent use of prayer, and from being more zealously moved under the pressure of some greater need. Of perseverance in prayer, which is closely related to diligence, we shall speak toward the end of the chapter (sections 51, 52). This diligence, moreover, is very different from the βαττολογίαν, vain speaking, which our Savior has forbidden (Matthew 6:7). For he does not there forbid us to pray long or often or with great fervor, but warns us against supposing that we can extort anything from God by pestering him with chattering wordiness, as if he were to be persuaded in the way men are. We know that hypocrites, because they do not consider that they have to do with God, offer up their prayers as pompously as if they were part of a triumphal parade. The Pharisee who thanked God that he was not like other men no doubt proclaimed his own praises before men, as if he wished to gain a reputation for holiness by his prayers. Hence that vain speaking which, for a similar reason, prevails so widely in the Papacy today, some idly spinning out the time by repeating the same frivolous prayers, and others using a long string of verbiage for vulgar display. French, "Cette longueur de priere a aujord'hui sa vogue en la Papauté, et procede de cette mesme source; c'est que les uns barbotant force Ave Maria, et reiterant cent fois un chapelet, perdent une partie du temps; les autres, comme les chanoines et caphars, en abayant le parchemin jour et nuiet, et barbotant leur breviare vendent leur coquilles au peuple." That is: This long prayer is at present in vogue among the Papists, over their beads a hundred times, lose part of their time; others, such as the canons and monks, grumbling over their parchment night and day and muttering their breviary, sell their cockleshells to the people.
Calvin translates, "Te expectat Deus, laus in Sion"; that is, God, the praise in Zion waits for you.

As God in his word commands common prayers, so public temples are the places appointed for offering them; and therefore those who refuse to join with the people of God in this observance have no ground for the excuse that they enter their own room in order to obey the command of the Lord. For he who promises to grant whatever two or three gathered in his name shall ask (Matthew 18:20) declares that he by no means despises the prayers which are offered publicly, provided there is no ostentation or grasping after human applause, and provided there is a true and sincere affection in the secret depths of the heart. See Book 1, chapter 11, sections 7, 13, on the subject of images in churches. Also Book 4, chapter 4, section 8, and chapter 5, section 18, on the ornaments of churches.

From this it is perfectly clear that neither words nor singing (if used in prayer) are of the least importance or count for one iota with God unless they come from deep feeling in the heart. Indeed, they rather provoke his anger against us if they come from the lips and throat only, since this is to abuse his sacred name and to mock his majesty. We gather this from the words of Isaiah, which, though their meaning is wider, also serve to rebuke this vice: "Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honor me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid" (Isaiah 29:13). Still, we do not condemn words or singing, but rather strongly commend them, provided the feeling of the mind goes along with them. For in this way the thought of God is kept alive in our minds, which, by their fickle and changeable nature, soon slacken and are distracted by various objects unless various means are used to support them. Besides, since the glory of God ought in some way to be displayed in every part of our body, the special service to which the tongue should be devoted is that of singing and speaking, since it was expressly created to declare and proclaim the praise of God. This use of the tongue belongs chiefly to the public services held in the assembly of the saints. In this way we glorify together, as it were with one voice and one mouth, the God whom we serve in one spirit and one faith; and we do so openly, so that each may in turn receive the confession of his brother's faith and be invited and spurred on to imitate it.

It is certain that the use of singing in churches (which I may mention in passing) is not only very ancient but was also practiced by the Apostles, as we may gather from the words of Paul: "I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also" (1 Corinthians 14:15). Likewise he says to the Colossians, "Teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord" (Colossians 3:16). In the former passage he commands us to sing with the voice and the heart; in the latter he commends spiritual songs, by which the godly build one another up. That it was not a universal practice, however, is attested by Augustine (Confessions, book 9, chapter 7), who states that the church of Milan first began to use singing in the time of Ambrose, when, because the orthodox faith was being persecuted by Justina, the mother of Valentinian, the night vigils of the people were more frequent than usual. French, "Mais il adjouste d'autre part, que quand il souvenoit du fruict et de l'edification qu'il avoit recue en oyant chanter à l'Eglise il enclinoit plus à l'autre partie, c'est, approuver le chant"; that is, but he adds, on the other hand, that when he called to mind the fruit and edification he had received from hearing singing in the church, he leaned more to the other side, that is, to approving singing.

It is also plain that public prayers are not to be offered in Greek among the Latins, nor in Latin among the French or English (as has been the practice everywhere until now), but in the common language, so that all present may understand them, since they ought to serve for the edification of the whole Church, which cannot be benefited in the least by a sound it does not understand. Those who are not moved by any reason of humanity or love ought at least to be somewhat moved by the authority of Paul, whose words are by no means ambiguous: "When you shall bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say, Amen, at your giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what you say? For you verily give thanks, but the other is not edified" (1 Corinthians 14:16, 17). How then can one sufficiently marvel at the unbridled license of the Papists, who, while the Apostle publicly protests against it, do not hesitate to bawl out the most wordy prayers in a foreign tongue, prayers of which they themselves sometimes do not understand one syllable, and which they have no wish for others to understand? French, "Qui est-ce donc qui se pourra assez esmerveiller d'une audace tant tent et brayent de langue estrange et inconnue, en laquelle le plus souvent ils n'entendent pas eux mesmes une syllabe, et ne veulent que les autres y entendent?" That is: Who then can sufficiently marvel at the unbridled audacity which the Papists have had, and still have, who, against the prohibition of the Apostle, chant and bray in a foreign and unknown tongue, in which for the most part they do not understand one syllable themselves, and which they have no wish for others to understand?

We must now consider not only a surer method but also a form of prayer, namely, the one which our heavenly Father has delivered to us through his beloved Son, and in which we may recognize his boundless goodness and condescension (Matthew 6:9; Luke 11:2). Besides warning and urging us to seek him in our every need (as children are accustomed to take refuge under the protection of their parents when weighed down by any anxiety), seeing that we were not fully aware how great our poverty was, or what was right or good for us to ask, he has provided for this ignorance; where our capacity failed, he has amply made up the lack. For he has given us a form in which everything that it is lawful to desire, everything that serves our good, and everything that it is necessary to ask is set before us as in a picture. From his goodness in this respect we gain the great comfort of knowing that, since we ask almost in his words, we ask nothing absurd, or foreign, or out of season; nothing, in short, that is not pleasing to him. Plato, seeing the ignorance of men in presenting their desires to God, desires which, if granted, would often be most harmful to them, declares the best form of prayer to be the one supplied by an ancient poet: "O king Jupiter, give us what is best, whether we wish it or not; but turn away from us what is evil, even though we ask for it" (Plato, Alcibiades 2). This pagan shows his wisdom in seeing how dangerous it is to ask of God what our own passion dictates; while at the same time he reminds us of our unhappy condition, in that we cannot open our lips before God without danger unless his Spirit teaches us how to pray rightly (Romans 8:26). All the higher value, therefore, ought we to set on this privilege, when the only begotten Son of God puts words into our mouths and so relieves our minds of all hesitation.

This form or rule of prayer consists of six petitions. For I am kept from agreeing with those who divide it into seven by the adversative turn of phrase used by the Evangelist, who appears to have meant to join the two members together; as if he had said, Do not allow us to be overcome by temptation, but rather bring help to our frailty and deliver us, so that we may not fall. Ancient writers: Augustine, Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 116; Chrysostom, in an incomplete work. See the end of section 53.
